extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, judges, prosecutors, and scholars studying English common law on market offences and patents
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the legal definitions, elements, and procedural requirements for the common-law/statutory offences of forestalling, engrossing (ingrossing), and regrating, together with what commodities are covered, evidentiary/indictment requirements, and an introductory statement on patents as limited statutory monopolies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forestalling (statutory definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the words of the Stat. 5 & 6 Edward VI. c. 14: 'Whosoever shall buy or cause to be bought any merchandize, victual, or any thing whatsoever, coming by land or by water, towards any market or fair to be sold in the same, or coming towards any city, port, haven, creek or road from any parts beyond the sea, to be sold; or make any bargain, contract or promise for the having or buying the same, or any part thereof, so coming as is aforesaid, before the said merchandize, victuals, or other things shall be in the market, fair, city, port, haven, creek, or road, ready to be sold; or shall make any motion by word, letter, messuage, or otherwise, to any person for the enhancing of the price... or else dissuade, move, or stir any person coming to the market or fair, to abstain or forbear to bring or convey any of the things above rehearsed... shall be deemed a Foresteraller.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal trait: intention to increase the current price of provisions to reap pecuniary advantage and injure the public. Two investigative branches: (1) nature of contracts by which one becomes a forestaller (must be for goods on their way to market at time of contract); (2) conduct independent of contract (early buying, motions to enhance price, dissuading sellers, spreading false rumours). Examples: a fishmonger may be indicted if he buys to enhance price as fish are being brought to market; selling corn 'in the sheaf' treated as forestalling; growing crops can be sold but buying growing crops with intent to prevent bringing to market (to enhance price) is forestalling. Words or rumours alone attempting to enhance price are punishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forestalling — required nexus of the goods/contract
rubrics_metrics.description: The merchandize purchased must, at the time of the contract, be on its way to a market. An indictment that fails to plead that the owner was 'coming towards the market' is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contracts made in a house out of the market for corn not in the market were held not within the statute; conversely, if the corn was in the market, a contract made out of the market could be within the statute. Emphasize factual pleading that goods were en route to market at time of agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forestalling — conduct independent of contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent acts (not involving a contract) that manifest an intention to enhance market price render a person a forestaller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include buying in a market before the customary hour with the intent to enhance price, spreading false rumours to affect supply perceptions, offering dealers higher terms to induce their withholding of goods, or dissuading persons from selling unless at an exorbitant price. The law assesses the actor's overt acts to infer motive; innocent purchases done in the ordinary course of trade are not impeachable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engrossing / Ingrossing (statutory definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute description: 'Whosoever shall engross, or get into his hands by buying, contracting, or promise taking... any corn growing in the fields, or any other corn or grain, butter, cheese, fish, or other dead victual whatsoever, to the intent to sell the same again, shall be deemed an unlawful engrosser.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key element: intent to resell to obtain an unreasonable profit (ex intentione ad revendendum). The bare act of buying up a whole commodity with intent to resell at an unreasonable price is a common-law offence. Quantity need not be national—creating artificial scarcity in a town/district suffices. However, large purchases in ordinary trade without an intention to enhance price are lawful; foreign merchants bringing victuals into the realm may sell in gross; fishmongers may buy all the fish if they sell at reasonable rates. Cases (e.g., King v. Waddington) affirmed that obtaining large quantities of hops with intent to resell at exorbitant profit was engrossing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regrating (statutory definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statute description: 'Whosoever shall by any means regrate, obtain, or get into his hands or possession in a fair or market, any corn, wine, fish, butter, cheese, candles, tallow, sheep, lambs, calves, swine, pigs, geese, capons, hens, chickens, pigeons, conies, or other dead victual whatsoever that shall be brought to any fair or market to be sold, and shall sell the same again in any fair or market holden or kept in the same place, or in any other fair or market within four miles thereof, shall be deemed a regrator.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also called chopper, jobber, bagger, higler, or huckster. The treatise notes uncertainty whether regrating remains a crime at common law; notable case (Rex v. Rusby) produced divided court opinions and no final judgment. Practitioners should be cautious: statutory language historically criminalized resale within markets, but modern common-law recognition is ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commodities (what items qualify as 'victuals' or covered goods)
rubrics_metrics.description: All articles necessary to sustain life, and everything used as an ingredient in making or preserving those articles, are treated as 'provisions' or 'victuals' and fall within the offences. The text enumerates corn, grain, butter, cheese, fish, malt, salt, hops, etc.; perishable fruits (apples, cherries, dried fruits) historically were not considered victuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial decisions vary on borderline cases: buying wheat to convert to starch, or corn to make meal, has been held both within and without the statute in different cases; barley bought to convert to malt has mixed authorities. Salt and hops are now considered necessaries and treated as victuals. Where a commodity is used in making a necessary foodstuff, it may be included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of guilty intent (mens rea) in indictments
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a question whether it must be averred and proved that the defendant intended to injure the public and acted with an evil design to raise the price; the weight of reason and authority favors that such an averment is absolutely necessary and must be proved at trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where bad intent is essential to complete the crime, it must be alleged in the indictment and proved. Cases support the requirement that proof of intent (that the acts were done with the design to enhance price) is necessary for conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and certainty required in indictments
rubrics_metrics.description: Great certainty is requisite in the indictment; vague allegations (e.g., indicting a 'common forestaller' without stating the precise thing) have led to acquittal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantities described by vague Latin phrases (e.g., 'cumulus', 'magnam quantitatem') have been quashed for uncertainty in some cases though allowed in others. Venue and precise description of goods, quantities, and the alleged intent should be pleaded with particularity to survive challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proceedings to punish offenders (mode of prosecution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern practice: proceed by preferring bills of indictment at the sessions or assizes, or by moving for an information in the King's Bench; it is usual to proceed by indictment. Historical procedures (e.g., Court Leet presentments) are obsolete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precedents and practice notes (cited authorities) guide framing informations/indictments; practitioners should consult precedents (e.g., Chitty, East) for form and pleading. Technical objections (venue, certainty, allegation of intent) may defeat prosecutions if not addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment, penalties, and post-conviction procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Offenders against forestalling, engrossing, and regrating (now prosecuted at common law) are liable to be fined and imprisoned. After conviction and before judgment, if a length of time intervenes the defaulter will be committed unless prosecutor consents to bail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different statutes historically prescribed varied punishments; under common law prosecution the court may impose fine and imprisonment. Where multiple defendants are indicted and only one convicted, judgment may be given against the convicted party alone; practitioners should note bail rules and timing between verdict and judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawful exceptions and defenses (licenses, trade purpose, foreign merchants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Purchases justified by licence, purchases made for bona fide trade purposes (e.g., to alter a commodity by trade or science prior to sale), and sales by foreign merchants bringing goods into the realm have been recognized as lawful exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: licences were a justification (Dawkes v. Hill); buying wheat to make starch or corn to make meal has been held in some cases not to fall within the statute; foreign merchants may sell victuals in gross. The decisive issue is the purchaser's intent—ordinary commercial purchases without an intent to enhance price will be unimpeachable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between statute law and common law on these offences
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute 5 & 6 Edward VI. and related acts were often considered declaratory of the common law; when later statutes repealed those statutory provisions, the offences nevertheless remained provided against by the common law (as recognized in cases like King v. Waddington), although the scope and existence of some statutory offences (notably regrating) at common law have been debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical repeal of statutes (e.g., 12 Geo. III. repealing 5 & 6 Edw. VI.) may restore the law to its pre-statutory common-law state; judges have repeatedly informed grand juries that though statutory law may be repealed, common law still provides against forestalling/engrossing/regrating. Practitioners must therefore consider both statutory text and common-law authorities and subsequent judicial decisions when assessing viability of prosecutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents — introductory characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents for inventions are a species of monopoly founded on grants allowed by statute law; they are limited monopolies beneficial to inventors and the community when properly confined, and the common law is not altogether silent on patents for inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise contrasts injurious prerogative monopolies with statutorily-authorized patents, noting that the law of patents 'springs' from statute and is moderated by common-law principles and judicial determinations. This frames patents as a distinct, regulated form of exclusionary right rather than the arbitrary monopolies of earlier grants.
